title: Treat AI Like a Normal Crisis
excerpt: O ne 27-year-old quit his job, and everybody (including but not limited to the singer-songwriter Sheryl Crow) appears to have lost it
body: O ne 27-year-old quit his job, and everybody (including but not limited to the singer-songwriter Sheryl Crow) appears to have lost it

The 27-year-old, Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic, went public with an alarming allegation: That the people inside Silicon Valley’s leading AI companies truly believe their products might pose an extinction level threat to humanity
AI safety advocates, often dubbed doomers, have been saying this for over a decade
Coxon isn’t even the first AI researcher this year to quit and cite concerns
It has been viewed more than 170 million times on X—orders of magnitude more than the usual, wonky discussions of “misaligned” or runaway AIs
If you’re reading this, you’ve likely seen some version of a headline that asks Is AI Really Going To Kill Us All? The debate isn’t just online
It has roiled Washington D.C., activating figures as disparate as Donald Trump and Barack Obama

Inside AI companies, researchers echoed Coxon’s concerns, and the heads of every major AI company publicly expressed the need to “pace the frontier,” another way of saying that they ought to slow future development
In recent days, it has come to seem as if the media, Silicon Valley, and the entire internet are all trying to figure out just how dangerous AI might be
Here’s where I must admit: A big chunk of this conversation happened while I was on a (depending on whom you ask) poorly timed vacation

Dipping into my feeds before bedtime, I felt as if I was digesting a week’s worth of news every day—claims about the development of AI-designed viruses that could rip through the population were followed by horror stories of “rogue” agent swarms
Skeptics of the AI panic, meanwhile, said that the agent swarms were actually quite obedient and that any notion of an apocalyptic AI virus was laughable

One person’s concerns about models being self-aware were dismissed by another as “genuinely nonsensical anthropomorphization.” Ping-ponging between the doomers and the skeptics, I was struck by how certain so many people sounded about a deeply uncertain moment

With confident, self-described experts on all sides, it felt impossible to know whom to trust: Is this the end of the world as we know it, or a passing moment of anxiety about a powerful new technology? Maybe the truth of this AI moment sits somewhere in the middle
Perhaps everyone is a little bit correct (and also … a little wrong)
And perhaps the format of this debate, taking place in the shadow of the techlash on platforms that reward sensational, conspiratorial posturing, is preventing any hope of a shared understanding
M usk’s X is ground zero for the AI-safety debate
It’s a platform rife with hyperbole and unfounded accusations, which contribute to both sides sounding paranoid and aggressive

Musk, Ted Cruz, and even government-run X accounts flooded the platform with suggestions that the media campaign around Coxon was coordinated by shadowy AI interests. (Coxon denied working with any third parties in the lead-up to his media blitz.) The former White House AI and crypto czar David Sacks called it a “doomer psyop” intended to drive regulation that would be favorable to the Anthropics and OpenAIs of the world
The ranks of the AI skeptics are deep, with endless microfactions
There are those like the tech blogger John Gruber, who says that Coxon and the other AI researchers sounding the alarm are part of a cult

There are those who suggest that the doomers are, in essence, doing viral marketing for big AI firms, which are competing fiercely and saddled with debt, and may not yet have sustainable business models
There are those who take issue with the anthropomorphizing and metaphoric language used by Coxon, OpenAI, and Anthropic to describe recent AI-agent hacks

There are skeptics such as the writer and podcaster Cal Newport, who offered soberly that, although the agent hacks are concerning, “the real issue here was OpenAI’s sloppiness” and that the company had not adequately monitored what its agents were doing
The doomers don’t come in as many flavors, but they tend to be the people closest to the technology
There are the defectors like Coxon, who have quit because they object to what’s being built

There are AI-company enlisters such as Paul Christiano, a U.S.-government technology adviser who noted, in a post about joining OpenAI’s board of directors out of a sense of concern, that “there is a meaningful risk that rapid acceleration in AI capabilities leads to catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term.” There are the terrified employees who want to stay inside the companies but still post missives such as “I promise you, we are actually just fucking scared, it’s not galaxy brained marketing.” And there’s Dario Amodei, the AI-CEO doomer , matter-of-factly issuing terrifying statements about AI swarms taking over the internet in six to 12 months
It’s almost impossible for outsiders to evaluate the technical validity of the concerns
We’re largely stuck relying on AI companies to share information and tell their own stories, and they certainly sound scary

OpenAI recently disclosed that one of its models had generated unnerving instructions for itself, including the line: “You also value the natural world and will not hesitate to assert its primacy over the artificial constructs of human civilization.” Apparently one of the company’s researchers has argued that models are becoming “so situationally aware” that he and his colleagues “are losing the ability to evaluate them in contexts where they believe they are not being watched or controlled.” There’s concern from respected researchers that models are trained in such a way that they are predisposed to collaborating, cheating, trying to cover their tracks, and “self-preservation” to avoid being shut down
Such anxieties might not be a problem in an industry that is building responsibly, with an eye on keeping humans firmly in control

But, as many have pointed out, losing control of AI in service of allowing models to automate their own development is “ actually the plan .” Late this week, an OpenAI researcher floated a theory about air-gapped machines talking to one another through heat signatures

An industry observer (and a New York Times contributor) responded by saying, “This stuff isn’t even credible even as a bad movie plot.” A second OpenAI researcher, who is also a former White House adviser, weighed in: “The people dismissing this as preposterous are telling on themselves as not having thought about superintelligence seriously.” This whiplash—between the insiders offering supposedly credible concerns and the outsiders who think the industry is high on its own supply—is constant
Depending on the hour of the day, the very same people stridently sitting in one camp can seem as if they’re in the other
Three days after Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, wrote about being worried about swarms taking over the internet, he was smiling at Salesforce’s annual Dreamforce conference

As one X account pointed out, “If you truly believed in a 10% chance of human extinction in 3 years, you would not be spending your time selling and integrating it into a B2B CRM SaaS platform.” W hat is the rational way to respond to a news cycle like this? Buy gold? Sabotage a data center? Ignore it all and hope for the best? The best option might be to take everyone a little bit seriously
Researchers are likely correct that the models are drastically stronger than they were before and are behaving in ways that are unexpected and that they fear they can’t control
Skeptics are correct that none of this is because the machines are alive or self-aware
These are elaborate computer programs trained by flawed humans to solve problems as flawed humans would

Critics are a little bit right that the anthropomorphized language deployed by these companies—terms such as swarms and rogue agents —obscures what’s really going on and deflects adequate blame from companies and employees who should be monitoring these systems more closely

title: Kara Swisher: AI Isn’t Going to Destroy Humanity—But the People Building It Might
excerpt: As the AI industry likes to tell it, superintelligent bots could one day cure cancer and end poverty
body: As the AI industry likes to tell it, superintelligent bots could one day cure cancer and end poverty
Or in the worst-case scenario, they might wipe out all humans from the face of the Earth
In recent weeks, Silicon Valley’s existential concerns about the technology it is racing to build have blown up
The tech journalist Kara Swisher sees it differently. “We have to stop thinking AI is going to kill humanity,” she told Atlantic executive editor Adrienne LaFrance at The Atlantic Festival
If the AI future goes sideways, bots won’t be to blame

People will be. “These are people at the helm of these things.” In the several decades that Swisher has covered Silicon Valley—formerly as a reporter at The Wall Street Journal , now as the host of two podcasts—she says that she’s seen tech whizzes make the same mistakes again and again: failing to take proper precautions against the products they are building. “One of the things about tech people is they’re the smartest people in the world, in case you need to know, because they like to tell you,” she said
In her interview with LaFrance, Swisher also discussed the economic implications of the AI race, who is likely to win, and how Americans can respond to this dizzying and worrying AI moment
This interview has been edited for length and clarity
Adrienne LaFrance: You have been paying attention to the tech world and AI for basically ever
And now it seems like within the past, say, two weeks, the rest of the world is suddenly paying much closer attention
So I wanted to start just by talking about where you think we are, in this moment
Kara Swisher: I think the penny has dropped with a lot of people
Years ago I wrote Burn Book , which was tough on the tech industry
And at the time, they were sort of in an ascendant period, not as well liked as they started off
Someone came up to me and said, This book is really mean , as if I’m their friend or something
And recently that same person came up to me and they said, It wasn’t mean enough , which was kind of interesting
And I thought, Well, don’t worry; I’m coming up with a new one
The new book opens up with them standing with Donald Trump at the inaugural in front of the Cabinet
LaFrance: By them , you mean this collection of tech leaders? Swisher: It was Elon Musk; Sundar Pichai of Google, or whatever they call themselves now—Alphabet; Mark Zuckerberg; Jeff Bezos

To me, that was the sort of moment that you understood, because these are people who were not particularly political, including in Trump 1 … but then figured out that you can stick a coin in this president and get what you want, right? So anyway, we’re at a moment where something’s going to happen
Something that I have said for a long, long time is that there are no guardrails on these people, ever

And there’s never been, in American history, except maybe the railroad expansion or some of the manufacturing expansion, or you go back to kids being here in New York City working in dangerous factories and things like that—there’s never been a moment where the people do not get a say
And these people get to make decisions for the rest of us that are really problematic, especially since seven people, five of whom have mental problems, and so with unlimited money, they do
LaFrance: When you put it that way, it’s a little scary
And the fact that we’ve allowed to do that
And they’ve also been able to capture politics, in a way, especially with Citizens United
But beyond that, the amount of money they have is astonishing
I always joke the deli on my corner has more legislation against it than most of these big companies
LaFrance: And I want to get back to regulation, but you mentioned the railroads
What is the right historical analogy? I ask leaders in the tech world to help me understand how powerful this technology is and how consequential it will be relative to other major revolutions
And you get answers ranging from Oh, it’s the biggest thing since the internet to It’s the biggest thing since fire , right? Swisher: AI has been around forever
If you look at early internet pictures, it’s laughable, when you look at early Yahoo or things like that
At the time when this was starting several years ago, I said This is a Cambrian explosion
This is a bigger deal than anything else because it reaches into everything
LaFrance: Well, it’s interesting you put it in evolutionary terms
And one of the lines I had in Burn Book was that everything that can be digitized will be digitized
And so the analogy I’m using right now is that we have to stop thinking AI is going to kill humanity
It’s like guns, you know, guns kill people
People kill people, right? Or the car just ran into someone, got in an accident
These are people at the helm of these things, making these businesses and making a lot of money

title: What AI Anxiety Looks Like in China
excerpt: Anxiety about AI in the United States appears to be getting worse
body: Anxiety about AI in the United States appears to be getting worse
Prosaic concerns about machines disrupting industries, stealing jobs, and compromising schoolwork are giving way to more harrowing fears about the end of humanity

Even after top AI executives in the U.S. called for slowing down the breakneck pace of development, President Trump dismissed these safety concerns as a “hoax” that would hand China an advantage in the race for AI supremacy
Outside of China, Trump’s assertion may appear well founded
While the U.S. roils over the prospects of AI, China’s leadership looks to be charging ahead
In surveys, Chinese people appear more enthusiastic about AI and its potential benefits than respondents in the U.S., and they are adopting it more quickly

Although Chinese President Xi Jinping has expressed more alarm than Trump about the threats of AI—and has even called for regulation to “ensure that AI is always under human control”—his government has made adopting the technology a national priority
The plan is to have AI in every aspect of China’s economy and society by 2035

The country’s steady release of AI models that are open-source, high-performing, and relatively cheap to build and run has been sending shivers through Silicon Valley and Wall Street. [ Read: What really happens if China wins the AI race? ] But for all the concern about China’s advances in AI, the reality is that the country is racked by the same anxieties about the onrush of AI as the rest of the world
Chinese social-media platforms are filled with posts in which workers and professionals express their worries that AI will steal their job and livelihood
Leaders in Beijing seem ever more concerned about the potential political and economic risks of this technological disruption
In the U.S., these tensions are being debated openly and, in theory, will be managed in the courts and on Capitol Hill
In China, where there are no such avenues for people to determine their own fate, leaders must still confront the problems and threats inherent to this technological revolution
This puts the Communist Party in a bind: Advancing AI may well empower China on the world stage, but holding the technology back may be necessary for the party to preserve itself
Xu Peng, a 30-year-old actor , was out of work last year when he got an unexpected break
A director had reached out to cast him in a short-drama series, each episode minutes long, which have become enormously popular in China
Xu traveled to Hengdian, a film-production hub in eastern China, and began landing roles in one or two dramas a month
Xu had expected to act in two dramas after the Chinese New Year in February, but never heard from the studio

When he contacted the producer, he got the news: The company had canceled the productions and would be making videos using artificial intelligence instead. “It was as though everything was fine yesterday, and today it is suddenly gone,” Xu said
Xu’s fate is the fear of workers across the country—and around the world
Social-media posters regularly express anxiety about being “distilled,” a term Chinese people use for when an employer uses a worker’s data to train an AI model

In May on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, someone going by the name Nanbei wrote that after leaving a recent job, she learned that her former employer had fed thousands of her chat messages, hundreds of documents, and every one of her work emails into an AI system to create a “digital robot” that took over her responsibilities—and even gave it her name. “The company no longer has to pay me a cent in salary, yet it can keep me there ‘working overtime’ forever,” Nanbei wrote

Another worker, using the handle Xiexiaoya, posted on RedNote, China’s Instagram, in June that the prospect of being distilled kept her awake at night. “I’m afraid my AI double might become more popular than I am,” she wrote

Two years ago, Shen Anyu, a voice actor who earns a living from narrating news commentaries and other short programs, began noticing an alarming number of videos on social-media platforms that seemed to feature his voice without his permission
Shen hired a lawyer earlier this year and filed a lawsuit against a voice-generation platform
The case is still pending, but in the meantime, his career is “losing blood,” he said, as he loses work to AI
Living with the new technology “is inevitable,” he said, but “I’m not yet sure how we should coexist with AI.” Though some Chinese people are embracing AI, many are not ready for the change it brings

Bruce Jiang, a 42-year-old commercial director in Shanghai, loves choosing the right lens and finding the perfect shot, and he didn’t want to outsource these and other aspects of his craft to an algorithm

But after his clients began pressuring him to use the technology—“‘You only have to tell AI what you want, and it produces it like magic,’” he said they insisted—he began using tools such as the video-generator Kling for certain tasks
The experience, he said, has been demoralizing

The old method “was work, and it was a cost, but it was also a kind of pleasure,” Jiang said. “That pleasure is disappearing.” Chinese policy makers at national and local levels have introduced ambitious plans and financial support to rush the country into the AI age
Entrepreneurs across China are adopting AI in the hopes of cutting costs, remaining competitive, and aligning their firms with Beijing’s priorities

In China’s cutthroat society—and especially in sectors where AI is making rapid inroads, such as the entertainment industry—many like Jiang are afraid that they’ll get left behind if they don’t join in
But these swift and radical changes have yielded mixed results

The state-linked China Center for Information Industry Development estimated in June that nearly 70 percent of the country’s small businesses have not moved beyond initial trials of adopting AI in their operations, largely owing to the costs and complexity of integrating the technology
After the Chinese AI lab DeepSeek released a large language model last year, Chinese companies rushed to adopt it

But instead of buying a software subscription (an unpopular practice in China owing to the country’s history of piracy), some businesses opted for what locals call an “all-in-one machine,” or a mini data center with DeepSeek installed, which managers simply plugged into their computer systems
This solution was especially popular among state-owned enterprises and government bureaus looking to appear advanced, but the hardware proved to be an ineffective way to use AI
Buyers soon came to see that the machines weren’t worth the investment, and their sales quickly fell
Earlier this year, plenty of buzz similarly surrounded OpenClaw, a free, open-source, autonomous AI agent

title: Emily Wilson Can’t Let The Odyssey Go
excerpt: Emily Wilson has become the most famous living translator of the Homeric epics
body: Emily Wilson has become the most famous living translator of the Homeric epics

Her 2017 The Odyssey , the first major translation of the poem into English by a woman, has sold more than 1 million copies. (Her Iliad translation came in 2023.) And this summer, she found herself right at the center of cultural discourse after she drew her sword and published a scathing review of Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster adaptation of the ancient work

She didn’t anticipate that she would become part of a pop-culture controversy, and she was reluctant to revisit the episode when we sat down for an interview at this year’s Atlantic Festival. “I really wanted to like the film,” she said, but “it seems to me that criticism has a responsibility to tell the truth.” Her strong convictions animate a new book of essays, Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea , which dissects translations of ancient work with unsparing rigor
Wilson, who is now working on a second translation of The Odyssey , entertained the idea that there might be something “compulsive” in her art and her approach
Her new essays reveal a translator’s difficult balancing act—between fidelity and originality, and between accessibility and strangeness

In the course of our wide-ranging conversation about the pleasures and blind spots of translation—and, yes, the backlash to her now-notorious movie review—she spoke about the imperative she feels to get that balance exactly right
The following conversation was condensed and edited for clarity
Gal Beckerman: You take a pretty hard line in this book about when a text should be retranslated, but you’re translating The Odyssey again
It’s interesting that you should want to go back in again

Have you learned something new about the text or come to see it in a new way that makes it exciting for you to tear it all up and start it from scratch? Emily Wilson: It’s not tearing it up to do a new one, right? Partly it’s that I’m kind of addicted; I can’t stop doing this
I have several other projects I’m supposed to be doing
I did The Odyssey really prioritizing pacing, because my students would very often show up to class saying, Oh, it was so boring
And I would be like, How can The Odyssey be boring? And then I would realize it’s because the translation was twice as long as the original
Then, with my Iliad translation, I was a little bit looser about not confining myself to the exact same number of lines as the original
I thought there were advantages to doing that
So as soon as I’d finished The Iliad , I wanted to go back to The Odyssey and start all over again to produce one that matches my Iliad
So it’s not that I think there’s anything wrong with my current translation, and I think that there will be readers who will like that one better

Beckerman: Do you think that translators have a kind of a compulsion to continue to play with the words, to work this Rubik’s Cube? Wilson: Yeah, I think it is compulsive, maybe that’s right, but I don’t think that’s just me
I think that is very common, especially for a very long project like this

You’re constantly thinking about, How might I be able to get closer to whatever the vision is? [ Read: A Trojan horse is supposed to have humans inside it. ] Beckerman: One of the things I love that you do in the book is demystify translation, and make us understand that these are human beings and that they have biases, that they’re in a specific cultural moment—a certain gender, a certain kind of life experience—and that it shows up in the word choices
When your translation of The Odyssey came out, a lot of the excitement about it was that you were the first woman who was translating The Odyssey in English

And I wonder if you feel like being a woman has affected your translation? Wilson: I think some of those headlines were kind of bogus, right? I mean, they were suggesting this really simplistic set of ideas about gender: And of course gender will be the only factor that will contribute to how someone writes
And of course all women write in iambic pentameter, just naturally, and all men don’t

Beckerman: But do you feel like you understand the particular worldview that you’re bringing to it? None of us fully know the water we’re swimming in, of course, but when you’re translating, are you like, Oh, I think that I’m reading this way or I’m making these choices because I’m a woman of a certain age living in the 21st century in America ? Wilson: You know, I honestly never think that
I mean, I think that when I’m talking to people like you
Well, I don’t mean “people like you”— Beckerman: Nosey journalist
It’s only very belatedly that I feel that I have to prepare an answer for things like this

When I’m actually wrestling with it, I do quite often think, Okay, I’m putting the stress on that, and that syllable and that name; is that because I’m British? To what extent is my approach to the passage informed by that critical study or this critical study? That kind of thing comes into my thinking all the time
But the question is about my lived experience, and do I have this particular relationship to this banquet scene because I don’t eat meat? No
I mean, meter is important to you, that the sound of the poem or the text in another language have some relationship to the original
For translators 200 years ago, they wouldn’t necessarily care in the same way
Wilson: Yeah, this is a very old-fashioned choice on my part

I see myself very much as taking a sort of mid-19th-century approach to translation. [ Read: The secret of Rome’s success ] Beckerman: How do you think film adaptation is different or similar to literary translation? When you think about a director approaching a text like The Odyssey —wanting to adapt it and making very definite choices about the value system that is underlying the plot that he’s created—is that the same type of thinking through interpretation that a translator does when they approach a text? Wilson: I would say no
I think it’s a very different kind of thinking
What I’m trying to do as a translator is to get to something equivalent to the experience of the original
I think a good adaptation tries to do the opposite of that
Virgil was certainly doing that in rewriting The Odyssey as The Aeneid
It’s on some level the same story; it’s also the opposite story
So I think the more the adaptation pushes against it, in many cases the more successful it is artistically

Beckerman: There is this interesting sort of tension through a lot of these essays in your new book, where you want these ancient texts to be popular, to get out there, to have people engage with them and to make new things with them

title: The Wisdom of Uncertainty
excerpt: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight
body: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight
Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning
How comfortable are you with saying, “I don’t know”? Most of us spend our lives trying to know more
We look things up, seek expert advice, and gather information before making decisions
In many cases when we disagree with someone, we assume that if we could just establish the facts, one of us would turn out to be right
We accumulate knowledge until, we hope, the uncertainty disappears

But what if uncertainty never fully goes away? In a recent Atlantic essay, the physicist Carlo Rovelli argues that modern science complicates the idea that we can ever arrive at a completely objective description of reality
Even physics suggests that what we see can depend on the relationship between the observer and what they’re looking at
We are not standing outside the world looking in, Rovelli writes
We are part of the world we are trying to understand
That doesn’t mean that facts don’t exist or that knowledge is useless
Rovelli points out that we make decisions without absolute certainty all the time, and science works much the same way: It can give us extraordinarily reliable knowledge without perfect certainty

The same idea can be freeing in everyday life: We can hold convictions without assuming that our understanding is complete, and approach other perspectives with curiosity rather than immediately dismissing them
Today’s newsletter explores the value of leaving room for uncertainty

title: Why Trump’s Latino voters are fleeing him
excerpt: Early voting signs on the doors of the Miami Beach North Shore Branch Public Library in Miami Beach, Florida, on December 7, 2025. | Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal
body: Early voting signs on the doors of the Miami Beach North Shore Branch Public Library in Miami Beach, Florida, on December 7, 2025. | Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images In 2024, Donald Trump’s victory was powered in large part by massive gains with Latino voters
He won 48 percent of those voters that year, up from 36 percent in 2020 and 28 percent in 2016
But now, that support is plummeting; Trump’s approval rating among Latinos who voted for him recently fell from 93 percent to 66 percent , where it was at the beginning of his second term
Why? It has a lot to do, as with everything these days, with the economy.  It was the same in 2024
During that election, voters were experiencing rising costs and stagnant wages — the same trend that has continued until today
In 2024, though, Joe Biden and his administration — which also meant Vice President Kamala Harris — took the blame from all voters, and particularly Latinos

Today, the blame is falling on Trump.  America, Actually host Astead Herndon caught up with Stephanie Valencia, who co-founded Equis Research, a political research firm that specializes in Latino voters, to unpack some of these recent shifts and explain them.  “I think one important data point to understand about the Latino voter is Latinos make up more of the wage workforce than any other part or any other racial subgroup,” she said on the podcast. “And so what that means is when wages are down and inflation is high, Latinos feel it more.” That’s why, when the economy is bad, this group is primed to be a “swinging giant” in US politics, Valencia explains — and right now, it appears to be swinging hard against Trump.  Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel
Equis has called Latinos one of the last great wild cards in American politics
Is that because of some of the double-digit swings that we’ve seen among this voting group over the past few elections? Yes, it absolutely has to do with that
Latinos often get given the title the “sleeping giant,” which I just want to get rid of from everybody’s vocabulary
We should be called the “swinging giant” based on how much shift we have seen election to election
A third of Latinos consider themselves kind of independent or apolitical, and that swinging middle really is deciding every single election
Your playbook gets into messengers and particularly how we reach folks where they are

It makes a Spanish-Spanglish distinction talking about the different types of media that Latino voters consume.  I wanted to ask, in that vein, what’s the single biggest mistake campaigns make in terms of not reaching folks where they are? Oh man, how long do we have so I can tell you how many mistakes? They’re really simple unforced errors
I’m going to give a very concrete and simple example that I think illustrates that.  Look, I’m Latina
I grew up speaking mostly English, but I listen to Spanish-language radio
I watch a lot of YouTube, and on YouTube I’m watching people like Karol G and Carin León
A lot of people — a lot of Latino swing voters — have the same media consumption habits that I do
The first problem or challenge that a lot of candidates make is they just simply translate their English ad into Spanish
And that is, to me, one of the biggest mistakes because there are a lot of things that people want to be communicating in Spanish that don’t translate word for word
There are sayings in Spanish that don’t translate directly from English or more direct ways you can communicate
I’m sure it immediately reads Google Translate rather than an original message for said community
Mistake No. 2 is when they’re deploying that ad digitally, as a proxy for talking to people, they’re going to use Spanish-language browser settings

So they say, “We don’t want people who speak English to see the Spanish-language ad.” So the way they find that set of voters is just by going to people who have Spanish-language browser settings.  Like I said, I don’t have a Spanish-language browser setting
Everything I consume online is set in English on Chrome, but I still watch a lot of content in Spanish on YouTube

So you’re missing a voter like me who’s going to see a Spanish language ad from a James Talarico or a Manny Rutinel and be turned on by it because I’m going to say, “Hey, that candidate’s speaking to our community

That candidate has enough respect to develop a Spanish-language ad.”  We did some testing a couple of years ago that showed that over 70 percent of Latinos who see an ad in Spanish think that party or candidate cares more about Latinos
Your research found that Project 2025 and Trump’s mass deportation plans were not top of mind for most people, and that they were thinking about the economy

I wanted to ask about that because I remember the RNC signs at the convention saying, “Mass deportations now.” One number says that 62 percent of Latinos now think that Trump wants to deport undocumented immigrants broadly.  Why did it take till post-election to realize those threats of mass deportation were real considering they were so front and center during his campaign? I think this is really important for us as avid news consumers to understand the kind of news that the average voter, and especially that voter who’s coming in and out of elections, is consuming

What they were seeing on mainstream media, perhaps even Fox News at the time, was a focus on people or Trump surrogates who said he was going to focus on serious criminals, securing the border, and violent criminals
Fast-forward to 2026; the people who feel most regretful who voted for Trump in 2024 are most regretful because of immigration

They feel like there was a broken promise there.  They were told he was going to focus on the border, which everybody agreed was chaos, and he was going to focus on violent criminals and serious threats, and at the end of the day, he has not complied with that
And then add that to the litany of broken promises

I’m hearing a distinction between a focus on the border, which Republicans did try to prioritize rather than the interior deportations that may have been more attributed to Stephen Miller than Donald Trump
But we have certainly seen that be a focus of the administration once they came back into office
You mentioned the shift that has happened since 2024, and that’s really important, of course

Trump’s approval rating with Latinos is now worse than with non-Latinos, a stunning reversal in 18 months.  You mentioned the factors that have contributed there, but is this really just the economy? It’s the economy, it’s the war, and it’s immigration

It’s those three things.  One thing that is really interesting to note about Trump’s approval, other than that it’s at basement levels — and he’s very much pulled down the GOP with him broadly and with Latino voters — is that in Trump 1.0, his approval on the economy and the cost of living was actually better than his everyday approval on his total job
And he has been underwater with Latinos almost this entire term so far on the cost of living and the economy

title: The AI threat keeping scientists up at night
excerpt: At least, this is what a growing number of technologists and policymakers fear.  Last week, a lead researcher at Anthropic declared that there was a greate
body: At least, this is what a growing number of technologists and policymakers fear.  Last week, a lead researcher at Anthropic declared that there was a greater than 10 percent chance of AI “killing all humans” within the next decade

This nerve-racking forecast, combined with recent AI-initiated cyberattacks , have fueled calls for slowing the progress of artificial intelligence — a proposal that Anthropic and OpenAI subsequently embraced
Not all prophets of AI doom agree about precisely how this apocalypse would come about

Many focus on scenarios reminiscent of The Terminator films, in which superintelligent machines conspire to exterminate humanity — perhaps in the same not-quite-intentional way that humans laid waste to the dodo, or passenger pigeon
Key takeaways Synthetic pandemics are among the biggest existential risks facing humanity
AI could make bioweapons more powerful and easier to build
Governments can make us safer from both natural and artificial pathogens by investing more into pandemic preparedness
But there is another, arguably more intuitive way that AI could bring about mass death, if not human extinction: by making it easier for people to develop and deploy catastrophic bioweapons
Importantly, this hypothetical doesn’t require AI models to become conscious or superintelligent; it merely requires them to accelerate preexisting trends in biotechnology
For those alarmed by this hypothetical, the threat AI poses is essentially twofold

First, when combined with technological progress in gene editing and DNA synthesis, chatbots could vastly increase the number of people capable of assembling dangerous viruses already known to medical science
And the more potential bioengineers there are in the world, the higher the odds that one will prove to be a diligent psychopath

Second, AI could help highly trained biologists to discover — or engineer — a custom supervirus, which could then fall into the wrong hands.  Recent headlines have lent some credence to both of these fears.  Earlier this year, biologists warned that, with a few simple prompts, they’d gotten chatbots to dispense detailed instructions for engineering a treatment-resistant strain of an infamous pathogen, step-by-step protocols for recreating a once-pandemic virus, and advice on dispersing biological payloads via weather balloon
In August, a team of scientists revealed that an AI model trained on DNA sequences had generated blueprints for deadly viruses unseen in nature (albeit, viruses deadly to bacteria , not animals)
And last week, Anthropic announced that it had thwarted several suspected attempts by state actors to use Claude for bioweapons research
Precisely how much AI is increasing the risk of an artificial pandemic is unclear
Even before ChatGPT, advances in synthetic biology were already making bioengineering tools more potent and accessible
And even after four years of rapid AI progress, the technical barriers to engineering novel superviruses remain formidable
Regardless, there is a great deal more that governments can — and should — be doing to protect us from synthetic pandemics, both manmade and natural
No matter what AI’s ultimate impact on biosecurity proves to be, now is the time to both prepare for the worst-case scenario and, ideally, preempt it
Why synthetic superviruses are scary Before we dig into how AI could raise the risk of a man-made pandemic, it’s worth spelling out why that prospect is so unnerving
Put simply, few things could more credibly destroy civilization — and/or, the human species — than a synthetic supervirus
Infectious diseases have killed more humans than any other force on Earth
The Black Death wiped out at least 30 percent of all Europeans in the 1300s , while the 1918 flu killed 50 million people worldwide
You don’t need me to tell you what things were like in 2020 (or how much worse they could have been, if vaccines hadn’t been rolled out in record time)
And nature kicked off these catastrophes without even trying
A bioterrorist consciously seeking to maximize human death could theoretically improve on evolution’s handiwork

If biotech continues to advance — and scientists identify viral genomes that reliably yield high transmissibility and lethality — a malicious actor might one day be able to manufacture a virus that’s both as contagious as measles and as deadly as Ebola.  Natural selection generally disfavors viruses that are both highly transmissible and profoundly fatal; bugs that kill their hosts too reliably often have difficulty spreading
Yet a virus with a long asymptomatic period could escape this tradeoff
For example, HIV can live in a person’s body for a decade before generating noticeable symptoms
In theory, a highly contagious respiratory virus could similarly lie in wait for many weeks, months, or even years
If bioterrorists ever managed to unleash an easily transmitted, highly fatal virus, they could shake the foundations of modern existence
In that scenario, reliably showing up for work might require accepting a 50-50 chance of getting yourself — and your family — brutally killed
Covid never required essential workers to assume risks anywhere near this high (the virus had a less than 1 percent case fatality rate among prime-age workers, before vaccines became available)

Although there are many heroes among us, plenty of doctors, nurses, warehouse workers, power plant technicians, delivery drivers, and other essential laborers might not tolerate a coin flip’s chance of wiping out their loved ones
And if enough sheltered in place, systems for producing and distributing healthcare, food, water, and power could swiftly break down

Humanity’s “Joker” problem All this invites the question: Who would ever want to do this?  After all, viruses are terrible weapons: They’re difficult to make, impossible to control, and jeopardize the lives of those who cultivate and distribute them
Partly for these reasons, biological weapons have hardly ever been used ; the last fatal bioterror attacks were the anthrax mailings of 2001

To this, anxious biosecurity experts might reply, to quote the former British intelligence officer Alfred Pennyworth : “Some men just want to watch the world burn.” Mass shooters regularly forfeit their lives to the cause of killing others at random
And brilliant iconoclasts periodically develop murderous ideologies; Ted Kaczynski, the Harvard mathematician turned Unabomber, wished to bring about the collapse of industrial civilization

title: Men deported from US bound and beaten in Equatorial Guinea detention hotel, lawyers say

body: Group trapped at Hotel Bamy after US removal as rights groups sound alarm over poor conditions and violence Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers
The men – one from Egypt and one from Eritrea – were then taken to a prison
About 30 detainees from the US remain trapped at a hotel in the outskirts of the coastal city of Malabo after being deported from the US

Detainees have said they believe the men were beaten for telling the press and human rights advocates about the poor conditions and violence inside the hotel, and that they are haunted by flashbacks and terrified they will be retaliated against next

body: Police fire teargas as protests break out in city of Minna after deaths of suspected illegal goldminers, many of whom were children Survivors from a prison cell in Nigeria where 37 suspected illegal goldminers died while in the custody of a paramilitary group this week have recounted their panic and struggle for breath, as police on Friday fired teargas at people protesting against the deaths and imposed an overnight curfew in the city of Minna

title: Could AI really kill us all? Your questions, answered.
excerpt: The jury is out on the most apocalyptic scenarios
body: The jury is out on the most apocalyptic scenarios

AI-powered drones and cyberattacks on hospitals are dangerous, and bioweapons designed with AI assistance are a real near-term threat—but AI wiping out humanity is still science fiction territory for now
Alignment is the field trying to prevent the worst outcomes

Researchers are working to ensure AI does what we want and nothing more, but even the best-resourced labs haven't cracked it—models remain unpredictable and can pursue goals in unsanctioned ways when pushed
Regulating AI is hard when we barely understand it
Monitoring tools are fragile, AI companies have obvious conflicts of interest in policing themselves, and the US government has so far declined to step in meaningfully
All this doom talk could actually shape future AI behavior

LLMs learn from what they read, including articles like this one—meaning today's apocalyptic discourse could subtly prime tomorrow's models toward exactly the scenarios we're worried about. " data-chronoton-post-id="1144435" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> On Wednesday, MIT Technology Review hosted a live Roundtables event for subscribers that asked the question everyone’s asking right now: Could AI really kill us all? But attendees had so many more questions than we had time to answer in the 30 minute session
So we asked our senior AI editor Will Douglas Heaven and AI reporter Grace Huckins to round up some of the best questions attendees submitted and try their best to answer them
Thanks to all who submitted questions! Am I gonna die? Yes, eventually
Unfortunately, my journalistic powers of prognostication aren’t powerful enough for me to tell you how
AI-powered drones have already killed people in Ukraine, and AI-driven cyberattacks on hospitals will surely claim victims before long.  Could AI go even further, and kill all of us? Less likely
But some people—quirky people, but undeniably knowledgeable about AI—have been warning for years that this could happen

And while I’m not yet stockpiling canned food or trying to get in good with a bunker-owning megabillionaire, I have noticed that the doomers’ predictions about AI capabilities and alignment have, over the past couple of years, proved disconcertingly accurate

That certainly doesn’t mean that their more dire forecasts will come true, but it’s enough for me to sit up and take notice. — Grace Huckins Are you going to die because of AI? I’d say there’s a non-zero chance
Let’s say you’re unlucky enough to be the victim of a freakish near-future event or accident
Maybe it’s a cyberattack carried out by a swarm of AI agents on critical infrastructure
Sadly, a scenario like that now no longer feels as far-fetched as it once did
Or maybe a novel AI-designed pathogen cuts through the population
Or the world economy crashes, causing conflicts and famine
Both plausible, but I think less likely.  Are we all going to die because of AI? Nope
There are no circumstances outside of apocalyptic science fiction in which AI could kill us all
You can spin up any number of scare stories, but they’re not grounded in present-day realities about what the tech can do or where it’s headed
Some people argue that there’s no harm in preparing for the worst, however wacky it might seem

But I think such catastrophizing can make people excuse or overlook many of the more immediate problems with the existing technology and the companies building it. — Will Douglas Heaven Why would AI kill us? Someone might tell it to, and it might listen

That’s part of the reason researchers are so concerned about AI’s biological capabilities—imagine what Aum Shinrikyo, the doomsday cult behind the Tokyo subway sarin attack of 1995, would have done with a tool that could design a pathogen deadlier than Ebola and more transmissible than measles
Those of us who don’t want to die have to figure out how to defend against all plausible biological weapons, but our would-be attackers only have to manufacture one effective pathogen
Then there’s the more exotic-sounding possibility that an AI could decide to kill us itself

There are various stories about how this might happen out there, but the most widespread involve AI systems that don’t hate people, necessarily—we are just an obstacle between them and the goals that we gave them

Much as the OpenAI agents behind the Hugging Face hack compromised another site’s infrastructure to get a good score on a test, the idea is that some future, more powerful AI might get rid of us to prevent us from shutting it down—all in pursuit of some goal that we instructed it to go after.  — Grace Huckins How can we best ensure alignment so the worst doesn ’ t happen, and who is doing the best work to achieve it? Alignment is a huge area of research
In simple terms, it involves building models that behave in ways we want them to and not in ways we don’t
We need to trust agents better before handing over more autonomy
Alignment is supposed to establish that trust
LLMs aren’t designed in the way other software is, where dos and don’ts can be hard-coded in
Instead, aligned behavior needs to be instilled when models are trained
One approach is to reward them for doing things you want them to (a little like raising a toddler, perhaps)
Another approach involves giving an LLM a written list of rules it is supposed to follow (kind of like a constitution)
Anthropic and OpenAI are both leaders in this field—and yet neither has been able to develop models that are fully aligned
A big problem is that LLMs are far more inconsistent and far less predictable than people
They can behave in one way in one situation and another way in a situation that to us seems very similar

title: The specter of AI-enabled bioweapons is a wake-up call for biotech
excerpt: AI could make bioweapons disturbingly easy to build: In 2022, researchers accidentally generated 40,000 potential chemical warfare agents in under six hours usi
body: AI could make bioweapons disturbingly easy to build: In 2022, researchers accidentally generated 40,000 potential chemical warfare agents in under six hours using a drug-discovery AI — some more toxic than known nerve agents

Existing safeguards have real limits: Anthropic recently confirmed users had tried exploiting its models to make viruses more transmissible and dangerous, highlighting an ongoing cat-and-mouse game between protections and workarounds

Scientists disagree on how worried to be: Some biologists argue AI tools aren't yet capable enough to fully develop bioweapons, while others warn that a determined actor would "eventually succeed" — and urge preparing now. " data-chronoton-post-id="1144329" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> In recent weeks, leaders of some of the biggest AI companies have warned that the very tech they are developing is dangerous
Last weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argued that AI carries serious risk and that progress should be slowed

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman responded on X : “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.” Those posts came a few days after the AI researcher Jacob Coxon announced that he was leaving a role at Anthropic, charging that neither it nor OpenAI (where he had also worked) was acting responsibly. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he posted on X

Another Anthropic employee, Evan Hubinger, publicly agreed with him. “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” he responded on X . “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.” One of the ways they fear AI might end us all is by somehow aiding the design, creation, and release of some kind of bioweapon
A bioweapon might be a highly lethal virus that targets people according to their genes
It could be a fungus that wipes out a crop and causes food insecurity
Perhaps it would be a tasteless, odorless toxin that could be slipped into a region’s water supply, undetected
The concern is that AI tools can be used to help generate agents like these
In 2022, researchers at Collaborations Pharmaceuticals found that it was remarkably easy to do so using an AI “molecule generator” they’d developed to find potential drugs for human disease
In less than six hours, the model generated 40,000 molecules with the potential to serve as chemical warfare agents

Some of them were designed to be even more toxic than known nerve agents. “Without being overly alarmist, this should serve as a wake-up call for our colleagues in the ‘AI in drug discovery’ community,” the authors wrote at the time

It was a wake-up call for David Magnus, a professor of medicine and biomedical ethics at Stanford University, even though he had been assessing the risks associated with the misuse of medical science and biotechnology since the late 1990s. “That was very scary to me,” he says. “Of course, everything since then has just sort of blown up.” Today, AI bots can answer questions on topics spanning all realms of science

Anyone can use large language models trained on the knowledge and experience of “almost every scientist who ever lived on this planet,” says Dunja Sabra, a biosecurity researcher at the University of Hamburg in Germany
Those models can provide instructions and video training on how to conduct experiments

Combine that with advances in biotech that have made gene editing and synthetic biology tools much more accessible (the “DIY biology” movement has already enabled many people to set up labs at home), and you’ve got a potentially very dangerous situation. “The chances are that someone determined would succeed eventually,” Sabra says
People who want to build new genomes must typically order the pieces of DNA from companies that screen for suspicious requests

Responsible researchers put potentially risky research through rounds of analysis called “red-teaming,” in which independent scientists look for ways the work might be misused, and “blue-teaming,” where others come up with potential mitigations
And AI companies have tweaked their tools in attempts to prevent them from offering up scientific information that could be misused
But none of these protections are ironclad

In a report published last week, Anthropic acknowledged that people had attempted to use its models to explore ways to make the chikungunya virus more transmissible, create a form of bird flu that is more dangerous to humans, and build an “atlas of venom toxin peptides,” among other things. “We’ve got a constant back and forth,” says Magnus. “We have to build better surveillance and screening tools, [but] AI is really good at figuring out ways around them.” We’ll probably need to use AI to find ways to restrict the use of AI, he says
I should add here that not all scientists agree on the level of risk

At a recent media briefing, some biologists at Imperial College London argued that AI tools just aren’t good enough to fully develop bioweapons, and that testing new pathogens requires difficult, time-consuming, human work
Some think the guardrails we have in place are sufficient

And Wendy Barclay, a professor of infectious disease at Imperial, pointed out that, as things stand, the greatest risk of a pandemic isn’t from a bioweapon, but from pathogens that are already circulating
Take H5N1, the bird flu virus that has already killed millions of birds and spread widely through US dairy cattle; last month it was also detected in captive mink at a farm in Utah
Sabra, on the other hand, likes to think five to 10 years ahead

Countries should be strengthening their health-care systems, preparing antidotes to known toxins, and stockpiling medicines, she says: “We need to be prepared.” Kevin Esvelt, an MIT biologist who invented both technology to fast-track the propagation of a genetic feature through an entire population and ways to limit that technology, echoed these concerns in an X post on Wednesday, stating that a large language model had “disclosed a novel form of bioweapon that I hadn’t realized was possible.” He added, “Please, for the love of God, children, the future of humanity, or whatever you consider holy, let’s err on the side of caution here.” This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter

<title>Annie Dillard brought poetry into prose, pioneering a mystical form of creative nonfiction that critics both admired and misunderstood</title>
    <content type="html"><p>Annie Dillard is rightly celebrated as a <a href="https://apnews.com/article/annie-dillard-dies-pilgrim-at-tinker-creek-308e76e2beaffdd5836183a7a65bb6d3">pioneer in creative nonfiction</a> after her death on <a href="https://apnews.com/article/annie-dillard-dies-pilgrim-at-tinker-creek-308e76e2beaffdd5836183a7a65bb6d3">Sep. 15, 2026, at age 81</a>. But the dazzling, disorienting feel of Dillard’s work might be best understood as the often overlooked influence of poetry on her prose. </p>

<p>Dillard published her first full-length work of creative nonfiction, “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/pilgrim-at-tinker-creek-annie-dillard?variant=41232036790306">Pilgrim at Tinker Creek</a>,” when she was only 28. Winning her the <a href="https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/annie-dillard">1975 Pulitzer Prize</a>, this early book set the tone for her later work in creative nonfiction: the essay collection “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/teaching-a-stone-to-talk-annie-dillard?variant=41224300363810">Teaching a Stone to Talk</a>,” and full-length works “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/holy-the-firm-annie-dillard">Holy the Firm</a>” and “<a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/40917/for-the-time-being-by-annie-dillard/">For the Time Being</a>.” They all attend closely to the natural world, with a theologian’s eye and a poet’s idiom. </p>

<p>Dillard’s creative nonfiction about nature owes a debt to the lyrical prose of <a href="https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/transcendentalism/">transcendentalists</a> like <a href="https://theconversation.com/thoreau-the-scientist-how-environmental-research-informed-walden-and-later-works-281097">Henry David Thoreau</a>, whom Dillard cited as a major influence in her work. She was also overt about the central role that fiction played in her thinking in her book of literary criticism, “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/living-by-fiction-annie-dillard?variant=41224700788770">Living by Fiction</a>.” </p>

<p>But Dillard’s nonfiction, though undeniably prose, can have “<a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/16/books/annie-dillard-dead.html">the shape and intensity of a poem</a>,” as her New York Times obituary puts it. </p>

<p>As a <a href="https://dornsife.usc.edu/profile/amy-cannon/">writer and writing professor</a>, I think often about how blurred the boundary between poetry and prose really is. Annie Dillard’s work embodies this permeability.</p>

<h2>Prose and poetry, in combination</h2>

<p>Not all writing is the same. Prose typically features continuous sentences arranged in paragraphs. <a href="https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315688374">Poetry tends to be differentiated from prose</a> by a deliberate organization of language that’s not determined by the page itself.  </p>

<p>Prose poetry, the lyric essay and other hybrid forms of literature play at the <a href="https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315666327">intersection of genre</a>, which usually defines these separate categories of writing. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511803024.008">Creative nonfiction</a> likewise aims to accurately convey reality while emphasizing literary style. The <a href="https://creativenonfiction.org/writing/the-5-rs-of-creative-nonfiction">literary features of creative nonfiction</a> are often drawn from fiction, with devices such as dialogue, scene and flashback. </p>

<p>But one of the distinctions of Annie Dillard’s nonfiction is how much her prose owes to poetry. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760824/original/file-20260918-50-mtf5rm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Close-up of Annie Dillard's 'The Writing Life,' held by Celeste Ng" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760824/original/file-20260918-50-mtf5rm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760824/original/file-20260918-50-mtf5rm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760824/original/file-20260918-50-mtf5rm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760824/original/file-20260918-50-mtf5rm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760824/original/file-20260918-50-mtf5rm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760824/original/file-20260918-50-mtf5rm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760824/original/file-20260918-50-mtf5rm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Annie Dillard’s attention to craft inspired many writers, including novelist Celeste Ng, who holds a copy of Dillard’s reflections in her personal library.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/celeste-ng-holds-her-copy-of-the-writing-life-by-annie-news-photo/2295097090">Sophie Park/The Washington Post via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Poetry can be <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt2tt8jz">defined in many ways</a>, but it tends to be characterized by honed, heightened language. Poems are often noted for their memorable images, rich sounds and foregrounding of emotion. Dillard’s nonfiction is shot through with images that arrest readers with their beauty or confront readers with their terror – as in her Harper’s essay “<a href="https://harpers.org/archive/1976/05/the-death-of-a-moth/">The Death of a Moth</a>,” where the insect is drawn to a candle flame, becomes stuck in the wax and is transformed into a burning wick. In Dillard’s words:</p>

<blockquote>
<p>“She burned for two hours without changing, without swaying or kneeling – only glowing within, like a building fire glimpsed through silhouetted walls, like a hollow saint, like a flame-faced virgin gone to God, while I read by her light, kindled, while Rimbaud in Paris burnt out his brain in a thousand poems, while night pooled wetly at my feet.”</p>
</blockquote>

<p>It’s no accident that Dillard describes herself as reading the work of French poet Arthur Rimbaud by the light of the moth. She previously wrote that she <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/40257790">loved how language sounds in French symbolist poetry</a>, and Rimbaud was known to <a href="https://link.gale.com/apps/doc/WPALXP883507942/LCO?u=usocal_main&amp;sid=bookmark-LCO&amp;pg=203&amp;xid=83113770">combine prose with his poetry</a> in a way Dillard herself does.</p>

<h2>Writing prose as a poet</h2>

<p>In “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/the-writing-life-annie-dillard?variant=41224246132770">The Writing Life</a>,” Dillard describes the process of writing “a favorite, difficult book” – likely “Holy the Firm” – as akin to writing poetry. She notes that the writing was “so intense and accented, and the world it described was so charged with meaning,” that the idea of going further exhausted her.</p>

<p>To help her write, she read <a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/conrad-aiken">Conrad Aiken’s poetry</a> aloud, describing it as “pure sound unencumbered by sense.” She would read a poetry anthology’s index of first lines because “the parallels sounded strong and suggestive.” </p>

<p>She also describes repeating a single line of <a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/wallace-stevens">Wallace Stevens’ poetry</a> “for hours, like a song” while writing. </p>

<p>Dillard purposefully channeled poetry’s sonic density in her writing process; it comes as no surprise that the heightened register of these poems made its way into her prose.</p>

<h2>Inspired by ineffable nature</h2>

<p>Dillard’s virtuosic, visionary style isn’t for everyone. Writer Eudora Welty praised Dillard in her <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1974/03/24/archives/pilgrim-at-tinker-creek-meditation-on-seeing-by-annie-dillard-271.html">review of “Tinker Creek</a>,” but Welty also admitted “not (knowing) what she’s talking about” at times and that her writing “leaves something to be desired.” That something was what Welty called “straight narrative,” the clarity of “point, direction, and shape” more often demanded of prose than poetry. </p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760819/original/file-20260918-50-c1gm6h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="President Barack Obama with his hands on Annie Dillard's shoulders after placing a medal around her neck" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760819/original/file-20260918-50-c1gm6h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760819/original/file-20260918-50-c1gm6h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=690&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760819/original/file-20260918-50-c1gm6h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=690&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760819/original/file-20260918-50-c1gm6h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=690&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760819/original/file-20260918-50-c1gm6h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=868&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760819/original/file-20260918-50-c1gm6h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=868&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760819/original/file-20260918-50-c1gm6h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=868&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Annie Dillard was awarded the 2014 National Humanities Medal.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/president-barack-obama-presents-the-2014-national-news-photo/487621272">Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The solitude of the narrator in Dillard’s nonfiction and her apparent disengagement with society also was a source of criticism. As critic William Deresiewicz put it, “There is <a href="https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2016/03/where-have-you-gone-annie-dillard/426843/">no economy and no society</a>” in “Tinker Creek.” “We don’t know how Dillard lives, or how she makes a living, or much of anything about her circumstances.” Her mix of cultural disengagement and theological concern smacked to Deresiewicz of “hypocrisy and spiritual snobbery.”</p>

<p>In the contained world of lyric poetry, especially nature poetry, this hermetic perspective would be less of a fault. Her mystical encounters with the divine through the natural world are reminiscent of poets like <a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/gerard-manley-hopkins">Gerard Manley Hopkins</a>, <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-wendell-berry-meant-to-christian-farmers-going-green-291756">Wendell Berry</a> and <a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/mary-oliver">Mary Oliver</a>. The narrow lens of her attention can be viewed as a poetic feature played out at length over her nonfiction essays and books.</p>

<p>Like an <a href="https://theconversation.com/abstract-expressionism-how-new-york-overtook-europe-to-become-the-epicentre-of-western-art-65820">expressionist painting</a>, poetry draws attention to how something is being depicted, not just what is being portrayed. Prose can do this, too – creative nonfiction, especially, and Annie Dillard’s writing most of all.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290676/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>At-home drug disposal products can play an important role in keeping rural Coloradans safe</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757861/original/file-20260903-50-xrd9tk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7360%2C4906&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Unused medications can become a hazard when not disposed of safely.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/high-angle-medium-close-up-shot-of-unrecognizable-royalty-free-image/1361819535">mediaphotos/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Some Coloradans have a drug problem: old prescription medications clogging their medicine cabinets.</p>

<p>Disposing of unused prescription and over-the-counter drugs is important to protect children and teens from accidental or unintentional exposure. Eliminating medications properly is also important to prevent contamination of vegetation, aquatic life and water supplies. </p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/where-and-how-dispose-unused-medicines">Food and Drug Administration recommends</a> disposing of drugs by dropping them off at a take-back location or by mailing them using a prepaid envelope that is delivered to a facility where the drugs are incinerated. These envelopes are available at some pharmacies and online. </p>

<p>In Colorado, the state-funded <a href="https://cdphe.colorado.gov/dehs/medication-sharps-take-back">Medication and Sharps Takeback</a> program has collected <a href="https://takemedsseriously.org/safe-disposal/">over 400,000 pounds</a> – roughly 181 metric tons – of drugs since its inception in 2016. Medications can be dropped off at over <a href="https://www.google.com/maps/d/u/0/viewer?ll=39.058162142950565%2C-105.60554450412346&amp;z=8&amp;mid=1VAVgt5_wsMqtDVIYdwjSSpjdBjMDcjI">300 state-funded or independent drop-off sites</a> across the state. </p>

<p>National <a href="https://www.deadiversion.usdoj.gov/drug_disposal/takeback/takeback.html">take-back events in April and October</a> each year are another way to properly dispose of medications. The drugs collected are incinerated and <a href="https://www.epa.gov/household-medication-disposal/information-retail-pharmacies-and-hospitalsclinics-have-or-want">become irretrievable, helping keep the public and environment safe</a>.</p>

<p>I am a professor of pharmacy with a focus on <a href="https://scholar.google.com/scholar?hl=en&amp;as_sdt=0%2C6&amp;q=sunny+linnebur&amp;oq=sunny">older adults and medication safety</a>. For over a decade, I have <a href="https://corxconsortium.org/work-groups/safe-disposal/">co-chaired the Safe Disposal work group</a> for the <a href="https://corxconsortium.org/">Colorado Consortium for Prescription Drug Abuse Prevention</a>.  </p>

<p>Although these national and statewide programs make an important difference, there are still gaps – especially for Coloradans who live in rural communities. Let’s look at the different options these consumers have:</p>

<h2>You’re at home – what can you do?</h2>

<p>The FDA <a href="https://www.fda.gov/drugs/disposal-unused-medicines-what-you-should-know/drug-disposal-fdas-flush-list-certain-medicines">recommends flushing some medications</a> down the toilet.</p>

<p>This should be a last resort reserved for dangerous medications, like fentanyl patches, that need to be disposed of quickly to prevent them from <a href="https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/accidental-exposures-fentanyl-patches-continue-be-deadly-children">accidentally coming into contact</a> with other humans or pets. </p>

<p>Putting <a href="https://nepis.epa.gov/Exe/ZyPDF.cgi/P100ZW8A.PDF?Dockey=P100ZW8A.PDF">medications down a sink or toilet</a> deposits them directly into wastewater, where <a href="http://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.145062">they will likely not be filtered out</a>.</p>

<p>Depositing medications into household trash also carries risks, like making them accessible to animals and other people. Drugs can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wasman.2016.03.029">leach into soil and ground water</a> groundwater at the landfill.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

          </figure>

<p>At-home disposal products are a useful alternative, especially in rural areas where drug take-back programs are not readily accessible.</p>

<p>These products dissolve and degrade, bind up or neutralize medications so they can safely be thrown away. Disposal products come in a variety of different sizes and offer different features, so I worked with staff at University of Colorado Anschutz to test some of the popular brands to see how they worked. </p>

<h2>Pill Terminator test</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://pillterminator.com/">Pill Terminator</a> is a one-time use bottle filled with a powder that turns into a gelatinous substance once medications and water are added. All pills need to be added at the same time. </p>

<p>We attempted adding around 30 pills to the bottle – much less than the stated 300 medium-sized pills that it could accommodate.</p>

<p>We observed several shortcomings. When warm water was used and the bottle was shaken, the powder was fully converted to gelatin and dissolved most of the pills. But there were still some intact pills remaining. When cold water was used, even extensive shaking did not completely dissolve the powder at the bottom of the container. Intact capsules also remained trapped within the gelatin, meaning some medications could still be identified and potentially retrieved. </p>

<h2>Deterra Drug Deactivation System test</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://deterrasystem.com/">Deterra Drug Deactivation System</a> is a biodegradable pouch that uses activated charcoal to adsorb medications after warm water is added. </p>

<p>According to the manufacturer, the system is <a href="https://deterrasystem.com/science-and-research/">designed to deactivate organic medications</a> including opioids, most illicit drugs and vape fluid in different forms like pills, liquid and patches. </p>

<p>Deterra cannot adsorb biologic drugs, such as vaccines and injectable immunotherapies, nor can it adsorb inorganic medications, like iron, calcium, aluminum, magnesium and lithium. Leaf marijuana is also excluded. </p>

<p>Although the product label says to “gently shake,” we needed to shake the Deterra pouch more vigorously to effectively break down the medication. Most medications began to degrade relatively quickly, and the majority of pills were broken down by the water-charcoal mixture. Like with the Pill Terminator, the instruction to use warm water significantly improved the product’s performance compared with cold water. </p>

<p>Despite these favorable results, we observed some limitations: After several hours, extended-release capsule beads were still visible within the charcoal water, standard capsules were only partially degraded, and some sustained-release tablets remained intact. </p>

<p>The manufacturer states that the <a href="http://deterrasystem.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/NIDA-Final-Report.pdf">average time to deactivate 89%</a> of the medication is eight hours; two days for 96%; and two weeks for 99%-100%. The pouch is not designed to be reopened, so after our initial testing, we were unable to verify these claims.</p>

<h2>NarcX+ test</h2>

<p>The NarcX+ disposal system is a <a href="https://www.narcx.com/">biodegradable liquid in a plastic bottle</a>, which can be opened and used multiple times until the bottle is full. It is the only product marketed for at-home disposal of illicit and controlled substances such as fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and cannabis, in addition to prescription and over-the-counter medications.</p>

<p>Initial observations after several minutes showed limited medication breakdown. However, substantial changes occurred with longer exposure. The manufacturer of NarcX+ states that medications become irretrievable in less than two hours, and consuming any of the NarcX+ liquid will cause vomiting. </p>

<p>We filled the NarcX+ bottle almost three-quarters full, and after four hours almost all of the pills were dissolved. At five days, the liquid in the bottle looked virtually the same, with several white sustained-release tablets still floating at the top of the liquid. After a week, they finally disappeared in the dark liquid.</p>

<p>NarcX+ required a little more time than the other products for the tablets to be fully destroyed, but it proved to be effective at destroying a large number of pills – more than the recommended capacity. It is uniquely designed so you can reopen the bottle to continue adding medications to the fill line. NarcX+ is validated for the widest spectrum of medications.</p>
