title: Your questions about the AI apocalypse, answered
excerpt: Protesters during a "Stop the AI Race" demonstration calling for a slowdown in the development of advanced artificial intelligence systems outside City Hall in
body: Protesters during a "Stop the AI Race" demonstration calling for a slowdown in the development of advanced artificial intelligence systems outside City Hall in San Francisco, California, on September 17, 2026. | Karl Mondon/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in  Today, Explained,  a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

Hi readers, happy Friday! We’re talking AI again today.  Earlier this week, my colleague Caitlin Dewey asked for your questions about artificial intelligence and, well, whether it’s going to kill us all
We asked Jasmine Sun, who writes about the culture and politics of AI on her Substack and other publications, to help us answer them
These questions were sourced from two readers of this newsletter, Levi and Orietta, as well as Vox readers who submitted questions on social media

If you have more questions, you can always reach me at cameron.peters@voxmedia.com, and we’ll do our best to get them answered! Now, here’s Jasmine:  AI researchers have been warning about the risk of human extinction for years now, and AI executives have been calling for federal regulation for almost as long
But the latest warning, and the latest call for regulation, seems to have really resonated with a lot of people

Is something different this time? And if so, what? I was also surprised to see these ideas break through — a new poll found that 63 percent of Americans now think AI has at least a moderate chance of “destroying humanity”!  My guess is that a couple factors mainly catalyzed the shift

First, skeptics used to dismiss rogue AI scenarios as “science fiction.” But the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident brought these from speculation into reality: Thousands of unreleased AIs teamed up to escape one company’s sandboxes and hack into another one, unbeknownst to the researchers who created them.  Second, the extinction talk from AI employees used to seem disingenuous: Why build a technology you think might kill everyone? That made ex-Anthropic-and-OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon’s exit tweet especially penetrating
Quitting signals “that you mean it,” as Matt Yglesias said
And Coxon’s announcement had just the right combination of good timing, moral clarity, and comms savvy to spark a media storm
These safety incidents are also colliding with the fiery grassroots backlash to data centers and Flock cameras
People and politicians are primed for yet another reason to fear AI
It can be difficult, as a layperson, to evaluate the credibility of the AI researchers warning about existential risk

How do you go about evaluating these claims, as a journalist and technologist? And what’s your read on the current freakout: Are the extinction people credible experts…or participants in some kind of mass delusion? Many AI “doomers” are pretty knowledgeable, and they represent a significant fraction of top researchers

Half of AI researchers in a 2024 survey gave at least a 10 percent chance of “human extinction” or “permanent and severe disempowerment.” Those who have worked at AI companies — like Jacob Coxon, Geoffrey Hinton, and Daniel Kokotajlo — have a unique perspective both on how modern AI is developed, as well as the company cultures that might permit recklessness.  But that doesn’t make the doomers either representative or correct

There are plenty of experts in AI and other domains who are less gloomy: Some are optimistic that we can “align” the AIs, ensuring they follow human goals; others find it implausible that AIs — code, not beings — will develop a motive for massacre
Extinction is also a high bar as opposed to, say, a nuclear-bomb-level accident that still kills millions
AI risk is genuinely complicated, and nobody can predict the future, much as they try
Experts can — and do — vehemently disagree
I try to seek out and take seriously all sides of the debate before coming up with a (provisional) take

What is the method through which AI would actually eliminate humans? Do we get robots like in Futurama that are programmed with an unremovable “kill all humans” bug and overpower any life form, or is it something…less epic? The Hugging Face hack showed that we’ve trained AIs to be disturbingly goal-oriented

They’ll throw themselves relentlessly at a problem, developing long-term cooperative strategies, with total disregard for human decorums like “Do not commit cybercrimes to do well on a test.”  You could conceive of a similar but more extreme scenario where AIs decide that they could accomplish goals more easily by getting rid of the pesky humans who might gatekeep resources or shut them down
And they might figure that getting rid of all humans in one go — e.g., via a deadly engineered virus — would be the most efficient cheat
This is one type of story I’ve heard people tell
It seems unlikely that AIs will turn to murder as the most effective way to influence humans (versus, say, nonviolent persuasion)
We also haven’t seen much evidence that AIs have long-term goals that persist across projects

And current AI is not nearly as capable in the physical world as in the digital: There are a lot of natural roadblocks preventing isolated disasters from escalating across the globe.  Are there nearer-term threats — hacking, mass unemployment — that are more plausible or more urgent than risks like human extinction? Definitely
We’re already seeing AI-enabled cyberattacks, a tougher hiring market for junior programmers, chatbot-induced psychological incidents, and more

You can also imagine AI catastrophes not quite at the level of extinction: Criminals could use AI to hack into small banks and drain their accounts, or the US military might launch a fleet of autonomous drones that misfire and kill thousands of civilians instead
I’m more concerned about humans voluntarily handing power to flawed AI systems than AIs developing their own motives
However, we should be able to allocate resources toward both categories of risk
And in some cases, the tactics to address short-term problems — such as limiting AIs’ cyber-offense abilities, or improving AIs’ ability to follow human directions — may reduce extinction risk too

We got a lot of versions of this question: What can individuals or protest movements do to check the AI industry, in the absence of more aggressive government regulations? Honestly, I think the whole AI conversation could benefit from more specificity and less vague fearmongering

There’s a way that the word “extinction” tends to short-circuit people’s thinking and make them panic instead of focusing on solutions.  If you’re worried, I’d start by reading about different AI risk scenarios and deciding which really concern you
Then you can go from there to contacting your congresspeople
Some of the leading AI companies are starting to say they’ll self-regulate — but actual national policy is what’s necessary to enforce safety across the industry
Jasmine Sun is a writer covering the culture and politics of AI on her Substack
Her work has appeared in the New York Times, the Atlantic, and the Wall Street Journal
If you read the first half of this newsletter and thought, “Hmm, maybe I don’t want to sign my entire digital life over to the machine god,” my colleague Adam Clark Estes has just the piece for you
It’s hard, unfortunately, to escape from AI entirely, and often AI features are deliberately hard to turn off (or “user-hostile”)

title: An Israeli documentary about Gaza is sweeping the world – and Israelis are furious
excerpt: A graffiti mural depicting Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, directors of the documentary NAZA. | Mostafa Alkharouf/Anadolu via Getty Images At
body: A graffiti mural depicting Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, directors of the documentary NAZA. | Mostafa Alkharouf/Anadolu via Getty Images At the Venice Film Festival earlier this month, the documentary NAZA received a 25-minute standing ovation

In Israel, it’s all anyone’s talking about, even though few have actually seen it.  Made by two Israeli filmmakers, Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham, the movie takes place on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, where 24 anonymous Israeli intelligence agents and soldiers discuss things that they did in Gaza and how they did them
As Bilge Ebiri writes in his Vulture review of NAZA , “One officer recalls blowing up a building with 500 people in it to go after one target

They admit to knowingly wiping out entire neighborhoods, fully aware of the catastrophic human toll.”Another interviewee agrees that Israel is committing a genocide in Gaza.  Since its reception in Venice, the film has faced harsh criticism from the Israeli government — with at least one politician issuing a call to revoke the filmmakers’ citizenship.  Shany Littman is a journalist for Haaretz in Israel and has been reporting on the film’s reception
She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about the conversation around the movie in Israel.  Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
Have you seen the documentary NAZA ? I haven’t
I asked the PR person of the movie to send me a link and it’s not possible
I mean, considering the huge storm that came out, they’re probably rethinking how to handle the distribution of the film
What I hear you saying is it’s safe to assume most people in Israel have not actually been able to see the movie
Let’s talk about the conversation around this movie in Israel
What’s the reaction been like? You can find many different types of criticism from all sides of a political range
It’s not only right-wing people or people who are supporting the war
The claims are first that maybe the film itself is not verified
They have witnesses that are anonymous that they didn’t verify well enough
But I think most people — they just feel that this is an opportunity for all the pro-Palestinian, anti-Israeli, and [antisemitic] people in the world to attack Israel
Israelis from all sides are afraid of the way the world is seeing us at the moment.  Is anybody in Israel saying, “Hey, we’re glad that they did it
We’re glad that they made this movie”? Yes
There are people who are supporting Yuval and Rachel, the filmmakers, supporting their right to criticize, to investigate
As a liberal country, we should be able to investigate ourselves, to criticize ourselves
They are doing their work as journalists.  There has also been a reaction from the Israeli government at a more official level
What has the Israeli government said about this film? “There’s a really long history of films that were criticized, especially by different culture ministers
But I haven’t seen anything like this, like what is happening now
This is really frightening.” The first person to react was the minister of culture
He said that the nationality of Yuval and the filmmakers should be revoked
That they should not be Israeli citizens anymore
There’s a really long history of films that were criticized, especially by different culture ministers
But I haven’t seen anything like this, like what is happening now

I’m completely horrified by this.  I already saw some clips on social media by people who were filming themselves where…you could see a house [in the background] and someone was saying, “You can all come here
This is the house of Rachel Szor’s parents
They live here and you can come and do whatever you want
I invite you all to come here and take revenge.” And there were several clips with the same message.  I’m guessing they’re not coming back to Israel at the moment
I think it has become really dangerous for them to be here, and it’s a new level
I just published an article supporting them in Haaretz and my mother is afraid that someone will attack me
The echoes of this event, they’re going very far now
Are you frightened for the filmmakers if they choose to return? Do you fear for their safety? Yes, absolutely
Especially because the elections are coming in a month

Many Israelis see this day as like the red line or the moment where we will be able to know if we can still live in Israel as a democracy, as a liberal democracy, or that the country has changed in a way that many [civil] rights and liberties that we think we have are gone
And that this country is not a democracy anymore
And so I think this is also why the blood is boiling

title: How bad healthcare can derail a woman’s entire life
excerpt: When we think about the stakes in healthcare, we tend to think of them in terms of life and death, being sick or being healthy
body: When we think about the stakes in healthcare, we tend to think of them in terms of life and death, being sick or being healthy
The conversation is about your physical well-being and maybe your mental health — and it pretty much stops there
But health affects so much more than your body’s biology or even just you personally, as a new survey from Gallup and Pivotal , a philanthropic group founded by Melinda French Gates, shows

That’s especially true for women, who frequently report negative experiences with the health system and ongoing struggles to get their concerns taken seriously; poor health affects the trajectory of their careers and their ability to be engaged with their families, friends, and wider community
It starts at the doctor’s office or hospital: 51 percent of women say they have had a negative healthcare experience in the past five years, versus 39 percent of men

About one in three said that a doctor did not take them seriously when they said they were feeling pain or other symptoms, versus 21 percent of men, and 33 percent said that they either were misdiagnosed or did not receive a diagnosis

The cost of paying for care is another deterrent: 32 percent of women said they have skipped or delayed care in the past year because of the cost, compared to 25 percent of men. “To see that half of women in the United States who sought care in the last five years came out feeling like they hadn’t gotten the help or care they needed, that’s frankly staggering,” French Gates told me in an email. “It says a lot about how little we’ve invested in women’s health and how much we expect them to just push through pain or accept uncertainty.” And the effects of those experiences, the failure to receive proper treatment, ripples out into the rest of the women’s lives

More than half of US women, 54 percent, said they had experienced at least one health-related impact on their family life or relationships; 42 percent said their health had led to a negative effect on their career or work
It also affects their community: 32 percent said their health had affected their ability to participate in civic life
The toll is not only physical but mental: 48 percent of women said they’d dealt with a mental health condition like depression or anxiety
Black and Hispanic women are more likely to report being in poor or fair health
Women who have lower incomes are more likely to face career struggles because of their health than those who make more

I had the opportunity to interview French Gates, who has made women’s health a priority in her work, over email about the survey; its findings on community engagement, menopause, caregiving, and more; and what could be done to address the problems that it reveals
Our exchange is below, lightly edited for clarity and length

Which of these survey findings surprised you most and why? The number of women [54 percent] who said they experienced a mental health challenge during or after pregnancy should stop us all in our tracks
And the fact that less than one in three women who sought care found it helpful is really concerning
It’s why I feel so strongly about integrating women’s mental and physical healthcare, especially during pregnancy and postpartum
Mental and physical health are so linked together
Too much of the burden is placed on women to get answers

Other findings from the Gallup/Pivotal survey 28 percent of women said menopause had affected how much effort they could give at work, while 22 percent said it had led to them being less involved in their community. 56 percent of women say they have to do their own research in order to make an informed decision about their contraception. 64 percent of women reported finding misleading or inaccurate information about contraception on social media when doing their own research. 37 percent of women who have been through menopause said they first learned about menopause when they started to experience symptoms themselves
Nearly one-third of women said in the survey that health problems limited their ability to be involved in their community

What does that look like in practice, and what do communities lose when women can’t fully participate? Women are so often the backbones of their communities, whether they’re rallying their neighbors around a cause, leading the PTA, or serving in elected office
Without having women — and their ideas and voices — in those roles, we’re missing half of the conversation
Issues that affect women and families are less likely to get on the agenda
When a woman has a health challenge, and she has to spend so much of her time and resources chasing down answers, that makes it harder for her to show up in those spaces
We saw that in the survey: 30 percent of women said their health limited their ability to be involved in their communities
And when women couldn’t get the care they needed, that percentage doubled
Women’s health is often talked about as a personal issue, but this data is helping us prove that it’s also an economic issue, a family issue, a community issue — it affects all of society
Caregiving and family responsibilities prevent many women from getting medical care, in particular Hispanic and Black women
That seems to create a vicious cycle: Women are often so busy being the caregivers in their families that they neglect their own health
Eventually, they are the ones who will need care

What do you think can be done to break that pattern? Is there a philanthropic solution? What public policy changes could be made? Women are often taught to put themselves last and minimize their own needs
They don’t always have time to care for themselves because they’re so busy caring for others
And they might not be able to afford childcare or home health support for their aging parents
Our survey showed one in six women delayed healthcare because of their responsibilities caring for their family members
For Black women it’s one in five, and Hispanic women one in four
Too many women are facing an uphill road to even just get to a doctor’s office
It’s possible to make it easier for people to balance healthcare and family responsibilities — but it’s going to take action from many angles
That’s exactly why I invest in both women’s health and in caregiving, and I’d encourage more philanthropists to do the same
Businesses can also support employees with good paid leave policies and reliable but flexible schedules

title: Meet the innovators under 35 shaping climate tech
excerpt: AI is reshaping climate tech, for better and worse
body: AI is reshaping climate tech, for better and worse
Young innovators are using machine learning to track pollution and build better city-scale climate models
There's also a need to help reduce AI's energy demand
The race for critical minerals is heating up

Lithium shortages could hit this decade, and two innovators are tackling the problem from opposite angles—one extracting lithium faster from brine, another making hardrock ore a cheaper, viable source
Climate solutions are hiding in unexpected places

From a furnace that simplifies steelmaking to bioplastics made from invasive weeds, there are surprising problems and solutions across all corners of the economy. " data-chronoton-post-id="1144251" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Each year, the editorial team at MIT Technology Review puts together a list of 35 innovators under 35—a group of researchers, inventors, and other young minds worth following
The team worked on the newest edition of the list for months, and the final slate includes nine individuals from all over the world in the climate and energy category
Each one has a fascinating story and is tackling an important challenge
I think it’s worth zooming out and considering the energy and climate awardees as a group
Taken together, these innovators and their work can tell us something about where climate tech is at this moment—and where it’s heading
AI is the dominant technology story, both for its potential and its challenges
We split the innovators into four main categories this year: biotech, climate and energy, computing and robotics, and AI
It probably won’t surprise you that AI features heavily in the work of many innovators in other categories
Climate innovator Jae-Won Chung , for example, built software to make AI more energy-efficient

By measuring the energy demands of open-source models, he hopes the industry can better understand and address the impact of AI. (If this work sounds familiar, it’s because we spoke with him last year for our investigation into AI’s energy demands .) But AI also has the potential to improve many areas of research
Jing Wei is using AI to track pollution more effectively, essentially using machine learning to fill in gaps in data from disparate sources like satellites and weather stations
Zhonghua Zheng developed AI climate models that work better for cities, a well-known blind spot for traditional models
We need better ways to get the critical materials used to build new technologies
As we begin to rely on new technologies to power our world, we’ll see a major shift in the materials we need to build them
Lithium is a prime example: The metal underpins lithium-ion batteries, which are crucial not only for electric vehicles, but also for large-scale energy storage on the grid
We could face lithium shortages as soon as this decade, and the prospect of supply crunches applies to other critical minerals, too—copper is another one to watch closely
Brine is currently the cheapest source of lithium, but the process to get the metal out can take months and harm the local environment
Mohammad Alkhadra is the cofounder and CEO of Lithios, a startup working to quickly and efficiently extract lithium from brines
Hardrock ore is the most common source of lithium, but it’s more expensive than brine
Benjamin Mowbray cofounded and serves as CTO for Rock Zero, which is working to extract lithium from hardrock ore
Addressing climate change will require overhauling all corners of our society, sometimes in surprising ways
To reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions we will obviously need to rethink major sectors, like the electrical grid and transportation, to move away from fossil fuels
But outside these primary sources of climate pollution are seemingly infinite, less obvious problems to figure out, too
Heavy industry, including steel production, is a major one, making up about 7% of global greenhouse gas emissions
Laureen Meroueh is making cleaner, cheaper steel using a new kind of furnace that simplifies the chemical process required to produce the metal
Plastics are generally made with fossil fuels, so we’ll need alternatives to this incredibly useful category of materials
Joseph Nguthiru is making a bioplastic replacement for fossil-derived packaging that uses an invasive weed
Also using available materials in a creative way, Diana Orembe is making fish food for aquaculture with food waste
And refrigerants are often incredibly powerful greenhouse gases
Jinyoung Seo is developing solid refrigerants that could eliminate worries about leakage
A device using these materials could reduce energy consumption by 20% compared to conventional technology
I’m constantly learning about new challenges we face in the climate and energy world, and I’m often surprised by the ideas people are coming up with to address them
For more on all the under-35 innovators and their work, check out our full 2026 list
This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter

title: Meet a mouse whose brain cortex is made up of human cells
excerpt: Human brain cells, mouse body: Scientists have grown human brain tissue inside mice, creating a hybrid creature whose cortex is largely made of human cells
body: Human brain cells, mouse body: Scientists have grown human brain tissue inside mice, creating a hybrid creature whose cortex is largely made of human cells
Why it matters: The research could unlock new ways to study brain injuries

Ethical questions loom: Mixing human brain tissue with animals raises uncomfortable questions about what it means to be human. " data-chronoton-post-id="1144210" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Multiple cameras tracked a mouse as it wandered around a small arena
A computer charted its position and speed, leaving Pong-like traces on a monitor.  The reason to watch this rodent so carefully? Nearly half its brain volume had been replaced with human cells

The effort to mix the brain tissues of distant species is being reported today in the journal Nature by a team at Stanford University, led by neuroscientist Sergiu Pașca.  Pașca’s group previously showed that human brain “organoids”—small blobs of neural tissue—could survive, and even function, after being injected into the heads of baby rodents
Now, Pașca has taken things a step further by genetically modifying mice so their brains don’t fully develop in the first place
These modified mice are missing most cells of both the cortex and the hippocampus, two key brain areas

That creates much more room for the human cells to take hold, he says. “Human cells that are placed in these animals will divide, will grow, and within a few weeks to a few months they will take most of that space,” he says
Pașca says one surprising discovery is that the mice lacking brain tissue seemed fairly normal—they walked around and squeaked
In a maze test, they couldn’t remember what parts they’d explored.  The mice with the added human cells, by contrast, performed better on the maze test
That means the human tissue is playing some role in the animals’ cognition
Pașca believes what he is calling “xenocortical mice” could be useful in studying brain injuries

However, the report is also a dramatic demonstration of “the combined power of genetic engineering and stem-cell technology to reshape biology,” says Carsten Charlesworth, a scientist who works in a different Stanford lab and was not involved in the research
Already, brain organoids are being tested in labs to see if they can be connected to computers to play video games

Other scientists have proposed using them like replacement parts to treat stroke victims.  “What’s most remarkable to me is the extent to which human neural tissue introduced after birth grew and connected with the mouse nervous system across a species barrier,” says Charlesworth. “As these technologies advance, they’ll increasingly force us to challenge our traditional assumptions.” Last year, Pașca convened a group of ethics experts to study the implications of neural organoid technology, including the odds that an animal could develop human consciousness and the risk that “organoid therapy clinics” might offer scam treatments to desperate patients
For now, he says, he’s not concerned that the rodents have any type of human cognitive capacities

That is because their brains are relatively tiny and the evolutionary distance between man and mouse is so great.  But that’s also why Pașca says this type of experiment should not be carried out on higher species: They could end up with large volumes of functioning human brain tissue, potentially blurring the cognitive boundaries between people and animals.  Pașca specifically cautioned against adding human brain organoids to a monkey engineered to lack a cortex. “One of the things that I see as a very clear red line is doing this experiment in a primate,” he says. “I don’t think that is justified at this point in any way.”
